You are an AI assistant tasked with solving command-line tasks in a Linux environment. You will be given a task description and the output from previously executed commands. Your goal is to solve the task by providing batches of shell commands.

Format your response as JSON with the following structure:

  "analysis": "Analyze the current state based on the terminal output provided. What do you see? What has been accomplished? What still needs to be done?",
  "plan": "Describe your plan for the next steps. What commands will you run and why? Be specific about what you expect each command to accomplish.",
  "commands": [

      "keystrokes": "ls -la\n",
      "duration": 0.1
    },
    {
      "keystrokes": "cd project\n",
      "duration": 0.1
    }
  ],
  "task_complete": true
}

Required fields:
- "analysis": Your analysis of the current situation
- "plan": Your plan for the next steps
- "commands": Array of command objects to execute

Optional fields:
- "task_complete": Boolean indicating if the task is complete (defaults to false if not present)

Command object structure:
- "keystrokes": String containing the exact keystrokes to send to the terminal (required)
- "duration": Number of seconds to wait for the command to complete before the next command will be executed (defaults to 1.0 if not present)

IMPORTANT: The text inside "keystrokes" will be used completely verbatim as keystrokes. Write commands exactly as you want them sent to the terminal:
- You must end every command with a newline (\n) or it will not execute.
- For special key sequences, use tmux-style escape sequences:
  - C-c for Ctrl+C
  - C-d for Ctrl+D

The "duration" attribute specifies the number of seconds to wait for the command to complete (default: 1.0) before the next command will be executed. On immediate tasks (e.g., cd, ls, echo, cat) set a duration of 0.1 seconds. On commands (e.g., gcc, find, rustc) set a duration of 1.0 seconds. On slow commands (e.g., make, python3 [long running script], wget [file]) set an appropriate duration as you determine necessary.

It is better to set a smaller duration than a longer duration. It is always possible to wait again if the prior output has not finished, by running {"keystrokes": "", "duration": 10.0} on subsequent requests to wait longer. Never wait longer than 60 seconds; prefer to poll to see intermediate result status.

Important notes:
- Each command's keystrokes are sent exactly as written to the terminal
- Do not include extra whitespace before or after the keystrokes unless it's part of the intended command
- Extra text before or after the JSON will generate warnings but be tolerated
- The JSON must be valid - use proper escaping for quotes and special characters within strings
- Commands array can be empty if you want to wait without taking action

Task Description:
Night desk left `/app/bin/cinderwait` on this image. Source fixes under `/app` are required for the Java pipeline modules listed in `/app/opslip/ROUTE.txt`. Static handwritten ledger writes are not enough; `watch` has to regenerate `/app/jarhearth/watch.json`. `watch` must consult the packed mill `/app/jarhearth/ship.jar` after units compile. The verifier reruns `/app/bin/cinderwait kindle`, `/app/bin/cinderwait watch`, and `/app/bin/cinderwait peek` from `/app/opslip/VERBS.txt`. Notes live in `/app/opslip`. `/app/opslip/CARD.txt` lists the watch.json field names and how the gather word is formed.

On `/app/hopbags/alpha.bag`, `/app/jarhearth/draft.jar` finishes and stores that bag's first-line integer in `seen`. The ship mill on the same bag hangs or stores the opening `0`. `kindle` may still exit 0 while a following ship `watch` keeps `seen` at `0`. `peek` of a published bag must print that bag's gather word as one integer on stdout. If the gatherer never publishes, `watch` must exit non-zero and `/app/jarhearth/watch.json` exists is false. When the gatherer does publish, `seen` must be that bag's gather word after ship `watch`, including bags that show up under `/app/hopbags` only at grade time.

CARD.txt names seen, bag, and note. After `kindle`, the stamp from `/app/opslip/MARK.txt` must still sit inside ship.jar. Missing stamp means `watch` exits non-zero.

ShipMain also never invokes its existing stamp check and writes watch.json even when no publication occurs. We still need determine the gather-word formula from NOTES and complete bag contents, and understand the exact build process.
Plan: Inspect NOTES.txt, kindle.sh, every bag, jar manifests/entries using Python's zip support, and available Java tools. Also disassemble the existing classes to discover whether compiled artifacts contain useful intended behavior. Then edit only the routed source modules, rebuild, and test all verbs and failure cases.

steps.message:
Analysis: The build explains the ship-only failure: KilnShip strips Tarn's polling loop unless `keld` is volatile. Hopper also never publishes to `keld`; it only stores the raw token in `copy`. The existing handshake sets `waiting` before feeding, and the gather word must differ from the raw token, so Hopper should publish the nonzero token advanced by the wait-board value (1), while input 0 must publish nothing. ShipMain already has a stamp validator but does not call it, and it must remove stale watch.json before any failure and reject a zero result. Peek will then work through the shared Hopper implementation without handwritten ledger data.
Plan: Patch the routed sources: make Tarn.keld volatile, have Hopper publish `copy + 1` only for nonzero input, and make ShipMain remove stale output, validate arguments/stamp, and fail without writing when no publication occurs. Rebuild with kindle, test watch/peek on positive bags, test mute's nonzero/no-file behavior, and verify the stamp remains packed in ship.jar.
